question_en: Which of the following instruments is least likely to be classified as a contingent claim?
explanation_en: Derivatives are classified as either firm commitments or contingent claims. A firm commitment is one that requires both the buyer and the seller of the derivative to perform some specific future action. All terms of this future transaction are fixed when the derivative is initiated. These are not contingent claims since the performance of either side does not depend on the occurrence of some other event. Most firm commitments involve a future purchase of some quantity of an asset at a specific price. A contract for difference (CFD) is a type of firm commitment that does not involve actual delivery. Instead, it is a cash settlement based on the difference between the contract price and the value of an underlying instrument at maturity. The underlying in a CFD is usually a financial instrument such as the S&P 500 Index that cannot be delivered. (Choice A) A total return swap is a contract in which one party pays the other the annual return on a specific bond, and in return receives a fixed or floating rate of interest. A total return swap is classified as a contingent claim since the amount of the bond's total return depends on whether it defaults. Therefore, the amount paid by the total return payer is uncertain each year. (Choice B) A credit-linked note is a debt instrument with an interest (ie, coupon) rate that is contingent on some other event, such as whether a different bond defaults on paying interest and/or principal.

question_en: An in-the-money European call option on a stock has 3 months until expiration. An increase in the risk-free interest rate will most likely cause the option value to:
explanation_en: Option pricing models and arbitrage pricing indicate directional relationships between option values and a variety of factors. Risk-free interest rates affect option values through their impact on the present value of the strike price. European-style options cannot be exercised prior to expiration. Consequently, their valuation reflects the difference between the present value of the asset (ie, spot price) and the present value of the strike price. Owners of European calls must pay the strike price at expiration if the option is exercised. Higher risk-free interest rates reduce the present value of that payment, thus increasing call option values (Choices A and B).

question_en: The lowest value of a European put option is the greater of zero or the:
option_a: strike price minus the spot price.
option_b: present value of the strike price minus the spot price.
option_c: spot price minus the present value of the strike price.
explanation_en: European put options can be exercised only at expiration. If the option is in the money, the intrinsic value equals the strike price (X) minus the spot price (S ). 0 If the option is out of the money, the put expires worthless with zero intrinsic value. The minimum value of a put establishes its lowest possible price prior to expiration. European puts can be exercised only at expiration, when the put owner receives the strike price for selling the underlying. Therefore, the minimum value prior to expiration must be derived by discounting the strike price to its present value.

question_en: Which of the following types of derivatives most likely gives the buyer a right but no obligation to trade the underlying?
explanation_en: Derivative contract comparison Forward commitments Contingent claims Contract Exchange of obligations Conveyance of rights Buyer has the right, but no obligation, to exercise; seller's Counterparties Both obligated to perform obligation is contingent on exercise Cost at Usually no cost to either party Buyer pays premium to seller initiation Examples Futures, forwards, most swaps Options, credit default swaps, total return swaps Derivative contracts are designated as either forward commitment contracts or contingent claims. Contingent claims are conveyances of rights in which buyers can choose whether to go through with the transaction (ie, exercise their right) and in which sellers are obligated only to perform if buyers exercise. Examples of contingent claims include the following: Options: Buyers acquire the right to buy (ie, call options) or sell (ie, put options) an underlying asset at a specified price at a future date, but the right does not have to be exercised. Sellers are obligated to sell (buy) only if the option is exercised. Credit default swaps (CDS): CDS are equivalent to credit options. If the underlying bond defaults, the CDS buyer can exercise its right to force the CDS seller to buy the defaulted bond. Forward commitment contracts are exchanges of contractual obligations in which buyers and sellers commit to a future transaction. Examples of forward commitment contracts include the following: Forward or futures contracts: Counterparties commit to exchange an asset for a specified price at a specified time in the future. A bond futures contract is a forward commitment (Choice A). Fixed-for-floating interest rate swaps: Counterparties commit to exchange a stream of fixed interest payments from the fixed-rate payer for a stream of floating interest payments from the fixed-rate receiver (Choice B).

question_en: A six-month European put option on a common stock is valued at €39, while an otherwise identical one-year put option is valued at €38. All else being equal, which of the following best describes the circumstance that results in this price difference?
option_a: The options are deep in the money.
option_b: The stock pays a dividend in nine months.
option_c: The underlying stock's volatility has increased.
explanation_en: Generally, an option with a longer time to expiration is more valuable than a shorter-dated but otherwise identical option. However, this is not always the case for a deep-in-the-money European put option since it cannot be exercised until expiration, and its strike price must be discounted by the risk-free rate to account for this delay. Due to discounting, a longer-dated put can have less intrinsic value than a shorter-dated put. In this scenario, assume that the stock trades at zero while the put option has a strike price of €40 and a 5% risk-free rate. The present value of the strike price, discounted for one year at the risk- free rate, is about €38. This is lower than the six-month put's present value of about €39. (Choice B) A European put's value increases if a dividend is paid since the payment decreases the value of the underlying. All else equal, the one-year put should be worth more than the six-month put, given a dividend payment in nine months. (Choice C) The value of a put is directly related to the stock's volatility, regardless of the time to expiration. In this case, the values of both puts would be similarly affected by an increase in volatility.

question_en: The exercise value of an in-the-money put option is best described as the strike price of the option minus the:
option_b: premium paid by the option buyer.
option_c: sum of the underlying asset price and the premium paid by the option buyer.
explanation_en: Put options give option holders the right to sell an underlying asset at a specified strike price at a future date. That right is exercised depending on the price of the underlying asset relative to the option strike price. If the put is: In the money, then there is value in exercising the put. Since the underlying asset's price is less than the strike price, the put holder can buy the underlying asset at its market price and then sell the asset at the strike price by exercising the option, realizing the difference. Out of or at the money, then there is no value in exercising the put. The strike price is less than or equal to the underlying asset's price, and the option holder lets the option expire worthless. The put's exercise value depends on whether it is in the money or out of the money: Put exercise value = Max (0, Option strike price − Underlying asset market price) If a put option is in the money, then it is worth exercising and its exercise value will be the option strike price minus the underlying asset market price, which is greater than zero. (Choices B and C) The premium is used to calculate a position's profit but not an option's exercise value. The premium is determined when the position is created and may differ for different positions involving the same option.

question_en: An increase in which of the following is most likely to cause the value of both puts and calls to increase?
explanation_en: Volatility refers to the dispersion of the underlying's prices around its average price and is expressed as standard deviation (distance from the mean). More volatility means a wider range of prices for the underlying, so call and put options both have the potential for higher payoffs. This increased potential can cause time value to increase, which adds to the options' overall value. (Choice B) A call option's strike (ie, exercise) price is inverse to the option's premium (ie, price an investor pays for the option). Options with lower strike prices are more valuable than otherwise identical call options with higher strike prices since the intrinsic value for in-the-money call options is higher for lower strike options. The relationship between strike price and premium is positive for put options; a higher strike results in a higher premium for puts. (Choice C) A high interest rate makes call options more valuable since the holder earns interest on the money that is not spent to purchase the underlying asset. By contrast, high interest rates reduce the present value of the expected payoff for a put option, so the put is worth less.

question_en:
An analyst observes the following market data for one American put option:

| Selected Data (in CAD) |  |
| --- | --- |
| Stock price | 48 |
| Strike price | 50 |
| Option premium | 4 |

This option's moneyness is best described as:
explanation_en: Moneyness refers to the relationship between an option's strike price and the underlying stock price and is indicative of the option's intrinsic value. An option trading at the money or out of the money has no intrinsic value. An option trading in the money has intrinsic value: For an in-the-money call option, the underlying stock price is greater than the strike price. This gives the call owner the right to buy the stock at a price lower than the market price, which in turn gives the option intrinsic value. For an in-the-money put option, the strike price is greater than the underlying stock price. This gives the put owner the right to sell the stock at a price higher than the market price, which in turn gives the option intrinsic value. In this scenario, the put option's underlying stock price is less than its strike price. Therefore, the option is trading in the money. Note that the option's premium is irrelevant to determining the option's intrinsic value; it would, however, be relevant to determining the option's profit at exercise. (Choice B) If the stock price equals the strike price, the option is trading at the money (ATM). At expiration, an ATM option is economically equivalent to owning the underlying asset. (Choice C) For a call option, if the stock price is less than the strike price, the option is trading out of the money (OTM) and has no intrinsic value. The same is true for a put option if the stock price is greater than the strike price.

explanation_en: A put option's highest possible intrinsic value is when the price of the underlying stock falls to zero (underlying assets cannot have a negative value). For instance, assume a put option with a strike price of 40, as shown in the diagram above (this is for illustration only—the principle applies regardless of the strike price). The option has a maximum value of 40 when the underlying stock's price is 0. Its value can only decrease at that point since the underlying price can only increase. Economically, it would be prudent to exercise the option but a European option cannot be exercised until it expires. In general, any option with more time until expiration is more valuable than an otherwise identical—but shorter-dated—option. This is not always the case for European put options: They cannot be exercised until their expiration date, so their value must be adjusted for the delay in exercise. This is done by discounting the strike price by the risk-free rate for the time until expiration. The adjusted put value is given by the following function: The present value of the strike price discounted for one year is lower than the present value when discounting it for six months, so the longer- dated option has less intrinsic value. Options that are at- or out-of-the-money have zero intrinsic value regardless of how long until they expire (Choices A and C). question_en: The exercise value of an in-the-money call option is best described as the market price of the underlying asset minus the:
option_b: premium paid by the option buyer.

explanation_en: Call options give option holders the right to buy an underlying asset at a specified strike price at a future date. However, option holders do not have to exercise their rights. Exercise of the option depends on the price of the underlying asset relative to the option strike price. If the call is: In the money, then there is value in exercising the call. The strike price is less than the underlying asset's value, and the holder can exercise the right to buy the underlying asset at the strike price, then sell the asset at the current market price and realize the difference. Out of the money, then there is no value in exercising the call. The strike price is greater than the underlying asset's price, and the option holder lets the option expire worthless. The call's exercise value depends on whether it is in the money or out of the money: Call exercise value = Max (0, Underlying asset market price − Option strike price) If a call option is in the money, then it is worth exercising and its exercise value is the underlying asset market price less the option strike price, which is greater than zero. question_en: When the market price of the underlying asset is 49, a trader sells a call option with a strike price of 55 for a premium of 6. At the time of the initial sale, the option is most likely:
explanation_en: Moneyness Call Condition Put In the money Spot price > Strike price Out of the money At the money Spot price = Strike price At the money Out of the money Spot price < Strike price In the money All options are classified by their "moneyness" (ie, in the money, at the money, out of the money). Moneyness is not determined from the buyer's or seller's perspective; moneyness is based on the price of the underlying asset relative to the option's strike price (ie, exercise price). In the money means that the option's exercise value is positive (market price > strike price for calls, market price < strike price for puts). Out of the money means that exercising the option would result in negative value (market price < strike price for calls, market price > strike price for puts). Holders do not exercise under such conditions, so the exercise value is zero. At the money means that the exercise value of the option is zero (market price = strike price for puts and calls). In this scenario, the holder of the call has the right to buy an asset at 55; currently, that asset has a market price of 49 (ie, less than the strike price). The holder could buy the stock more cheaply in the market than through exercise of the call. The option is described as out of the money since it would be irrational to exercise it.

question_en: A put option is most likely in the money when the underlying asset price is less than the:
option_c: present value of the strike price.
explanation_en: Moneyness Call Condition Put In the money Spot price > Strike price Out of the money At the money Spot price = Strike price At the money Out of the money Spot price < Strike price In the money Options are contingent claims that give the holder (ie, buyer or long party) the right to trade an asset at a fixed price (ie, strike price) at a future date. An option is in the money when exercise of the option allows the holder to trade the underlying at a better price than the current market price of the asset (ie, when the exercise value is positive). Call options are in the money when the exercise price is < the asset's market price. Put options are in the money when the exercise price is > the asset's market price. If a put option is in the money, the put holder can first buy the asset at its market price and then sell the asset at the strike price, which is > the market price, and realize the difference. (Choice B) A put option's strike price less the premium is the option's breakeven point. However, an option's moneyness is determined by the relationship of the underlying asset's price to the exercise price, regardless of the premium paid. (Choice C) The present value of the strike price is used in option valuation (eg, put-call parity) but is not a factor in determining an option's moneyness.

question_en: All else being equal, the value of a European call on a dividend-paying stock most likely increases with an increase in the:
explanation_en: Investors can have long exposure to equities by buying stocks or call options on stocks. Calls are usually priced at a small fraction of a stock's market price. The smaller capital outlay to buy an option means a smaller opportunity cost of capital (ie, forgone interest income) of holding an option (compared to holding the underlying shares). The higher the interest rate, the greater is this advantage. Therefore, all else equal, higher risk-free rates lead to higher call option values. (Choice B) All else equal, a higher exercise (ie, strike) price makes a call less valuable. Since call options give holders the right to buy, the higher the price that must be paid at exercise, the less valuable the right to buy. (Choice C) Dividend payments reduce call values: The stock price falls by the cash distribution per share, reflecting the decrease in the company's equity as earnings are distributed to shareholders and therefore not retained. The decrease in the underlying stock's price makes the right to buy it at the strike price less valuable.

question_en: An analyst collects information on three American-style call options on the same stock: The stock is currently trading at USD 40 and all options expire in one week. Which option has the greatest time value?
explanation_en: The option premium is the price of an option, which equals its exercise (intrinsic) value plus its time value. The exercise value is the underlying fundamental or intrinsic value of an option and cannot be less than zero; all other value of the option premium is time value. A call option gives the owner the right to purchase the underlying stock at the strike price and has intrinsic value if the stock price is greater than the strike price. If the stock price is less than or equal to the strike price, the call option has no intrinsic value (ie, zero). The time value of an option premium will decay (ie, decline) as the option expiration approaches. In this scenario, Option C is at the money since the stock price and the strike price are the same. Therefore, all the value (ie, USD 1.1) of the option premium is time value, which will be reduced to zero over the following week, when the option expires.

option_a: both call and put values decreasing.

question_en: Which of the following is least likely a characteristic of forward commitments?
option_b: Contract has a value of zero at initiation.
option_c: Buyer obtains rights, and seller incurs obligations.
explanation_en: Derivative contracts Forward commitment Contingent claims Futures, forwards, and Options and credit default Examples interest rate swaps swaps Buyer and seller exchange Buyer obtains right, seller Counterparties obligations incurs obligation Initial value Usually zero Premium Gain/loss Linear Asymmetric profile Derivative contracts are designated as either forward commitments or contingent claims. A forward commitment contract is an exchange of obligations between the counterparties. Contingent claims buyers have the right, but no obligation, to trade the underlying asset, and the sellers incur the obligation to take the other side of the trade if the contract holder (ie, buyer) exercises the right to trade. Examples of forward commitments and related contractual obligations include the following: Forward or futures contracts: Counterparties commit to exchange an asset for a specified price at a specified time in the future. question_en: All else equal, for a European call option on a dividend-paying stock, the call option's intrinsic value will most likely decrease if there is an increase in the:
explanation_en: The intrinsic value of a European call option is the difference between an underlying asset price (ie, stock price) and an exercise price. When the stock price is greater than exercise price (S − X > 0), the option's intrinsic value is positive and the option will be exercised. Otherwise, if S − X < T T 0, the option would expire unexercised. For a given exercise price, a rising (falling) stock price increases (decreases) a call option's intrinsic value. A company's stock price declines by the dividend payment amount to reflect the reduction in the company's assets (ie, less cash). So, an increase in the company's dividend payment would cause the underlying stock price to decline and decrease a call option's intrinsic value. (Choice A) An increase to the risk-free rate increases the value of holding the option instead of the underlying asset since it increases the opportunity cost of holding the underlying asset. (Choice B) An increase in the underlying asset price increases the intrinsic value of a call option since the option's exercise price does not change.

question_en: Which of the following best describes how exercise prices affect option values? Exercise prices are:
option_a: inversely related to call and put values.
option_b: inversely related to call values and directly related to put values.
option_c: directly related to call values and inversely related to put values.
explanation_en: Options are derivative contracts that grant specific rights to option holders. Option holders have the right, but no obligation, to trade an underlying asset for a specified price at a future date. Call holders have the right to buy the underlying and put holders have the right to sell the underlying. When the option holder exercises the right to trade, the counterparty is required to sell or buy the underlying asset at the contracted exercise (ie, strike) price. An option's strike price is one factor that affects the option's value: Strike prices are inversely related to call option values: The greater the price that must be paid to buy an asset the less valuable is the right to buy. Strike prices are directly related to put option values: The greater the price that can be obtained for selling an asset the more valuable is the right to sell.
